intro: George Robertson Sinclair, organist of Hereford Cathedral, has a bulldog called Dan. Elgar gives the dog a spectacular entrance: a tumble down the bank into the River Wye.

sections.label: Var 11 · Dan in the river
sections.mNote: Falling strings, paddling bassoons and a bark

cues.title: A bulldog goes swimming
cues.text: The strings plunge downwards. Bassoons and double basses paddle onwards in quavers. Elgar’s account supplies the action: Dan falls into the Wye, swims upstream to find a landing place, then scrambles out with a delighted bark.
cues.evidence: Novello full score, pp. 74–75, rehearsal 47. Elgar’s commentary assigns the fall to bar 1, paddling to bars 2–3 and the bark to the second half of bar 5: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enigma_Variations
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Sinclair sets a challenge
cues.text: Sinclair challenges Elgar to put the river incident into music. The composer is already fond of Dan: on visits to the organist’s house, he writes little musical sketches of the dog’s moods in the visitors’ book.
cues.evidence: Elgar recounts Sinclair’s challenge in his commentary on variation XI, reproduced at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enigma_Variations. The visitors’ book sketches are described by John Pickard in his BBC programme note (2005): https://www.bbc.com/radio3/classical/elgar/notes/note_enigma.shtml

source.title: Elgar, Enigma Variations, full score (Novello)
source.locator: Novello full score, pp. 74–81, rehearsal figures 47–51: the falling string figure, bassoon paddling and orchestral replies.

timeline.note: The strings plunge downwards in the first bar (p. 74).
Bassoons paddle in quavers; the winds answer the running strings (pp. 74–75).
Accented brass chords and percussion punctuate the wind and string phrases (pp. 75–76).
Clarinets and bassoons exchange short figures above the moving strings (pp. 77–78).
Brass and percussion rejoin the strings’ rapid figures (pp. 78–80).
A final string rush leads to the orchestra’s closing chords (pp. 80–81).

composer.epithet: He made the Enigma Variations from his friendships and preserved his own way with the music on gramophone records.
facts: His father’s Worcester music shop; violin and organ; composition largely self-taught
Powick bandmaster, instrumental teacher and organist at St George’s, Worcester
Two symphonies; violin and cello concertos; Gerontius; five Pomp and Circumstance marches
Master of the King’s Musick from 1924; recordings of his own orchestral works
composer.background:
Elgar grew up among the instruments and sheet music in his father’s Worcester shop. William tuned pianos and played the organ at St George’s Catholic Church; Edward studied the scores, learned several instruments and earned money with his violin. Born at Lower Broadheath on 2 June 1857, he had hoped to study at Leipzig, but the family could not afford it. His education continued in rehearsal rooms. Playing in the Three Choirs Festival orchestra, he learned the choral music of Handel and Mendelssohn from inside the string section.

From 1879 to 1884 he was bandmaster at Worcester County Asylum, Powick. He trained members of staff to play for the patients and supplied quadrilles and polkas for the Friday-evening dances. Here was an orchestra whose players he knew individually, with capabilities he had to accommodate. His other work included teaching in local schools and giving private lessons in Malvern. In 1885 he succeeded William at the organ of St George’s.
